title: Async streams and await using
cards/0/body: A method with async and yield return returns an IAsyncEnumerable<T>: items arrive one at a time, and you can wait between them. You read it with await foreach.
cards/1/q: Why is IAsyncEnumerable<T> better than Task<List<T>>?
cards/1/options/0: You can process the first items without waiting for all of them to load
cards/1/explain: You don't have to hold a million lines from a file in memory at once.
cards/2/explain: await foreach waits for each next item.
cards/3/body: The consumer passes a token with .WithCancellation(ct), and the generator method receives it in a parameter marked [EnumeratorCancellation].
cards/4/body: If cleaning up a resource is itself asynchronous (flushing a buffer to the network, closing a connection), the type implements IAsyncDisposable with a DisposeAsync() method. await using calls it and awaits it at the end of the block.
cards/5/q: How is await using different from using?
cards/5/options/0: It calls DisposeAsync and awaits it without blocking the thread
cards/5/explain: A plain using would call the synchronous Dispose, which can block the thread.
cards/6/q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
cards/6/options/1: yield return in an async method gives you an IAsyncEnumerable
cards/6/options/3: await foreach loads all items at once
cards/6/explain: Items arrive one at a time, and the finalizer is a completely different mechanism.
cards/7/pairs/3/1: Get the token in a generator
